verses.text: Now in the seventh month, Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the royal offspring  and one of the chief officers of the king, and ten men with him, came to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam to Mizpah; and there they ate bread together in Mizpah.

Then Ishmael the son of Nethaniah arose, and the ten men who were with him, and struck Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan with the sword, and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.
Ishmael also killed all the Jews who were with him, with Gedaliah, at Mizpah, and the Chaldeans who were found there, the men of war.
The second day after he had killed Gedaliah, and no man knew it,

men came from Shechem, from Shiloh, and from Samaria, even eighty men, having their beards shaved and their clothes torn, and having cut themselves, with meal offerings and frankincense in their hand, to bring them to Yahweh’s house.
Ishmael the son of Nethaniah went out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping all along as he went: and as he met them, he said to them, “Come to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam.”
It was so, when they came into the middle of the city, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah killed them, and cast them into the middle of the pit, he, and the men who were with him.

But ten men were found among those who said to Ishmael, “Don’t kill us; for we have stores hidden in the field, of wheat, and of barley, and of oil, and of honey.” So he stopped, and didn’t kill them among their brothers.

Now the pit in which Ishmael cast all the dead bodies of the men whom he had killed, by the side of Gedaliah (the same was who which Asa the king had made for fear of Baasha king of Israel), Ishmael the son of Nethaniah filled it with those who were killed.

Then Ishmael carried away captive all the of the people who were left in Mizpah, even the king’s daughters, and all the people who remained in Mizpah, whom Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had committed to Gedaliah the son of Ahikam. Ishmael the son of Nethaniah carried them away captive, and departed to go over to the children of Ammon.
But when Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces who were with him, heard of all the evil that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had done,
then they took all the men, and went to fight with Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and found him by the great waters that are in Gibeon.
Now when all the people who were with Ishmael saw Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces who were with him, then they were glad.
So all the people who Ishmael had carried away captive from Mizpah turned about and came back, and went to Johanan the son of Kareah.
But Ishmael the son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men, and went to the children of Ammon.

Then Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces who were with him, took all the remnant of the people whom he had recovered from Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, from Mizpah, after that he had killed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the men of war, and the women, and the children, and the eunuchs, whom he had brought back from Gibeon.
They departed, and lived in Geruth Chimham, which is by Bethlehem, to go to enter into Egypt,
because of the Chaldeans; for they were afraid of them, because Ishmael the son of Nethaniah had killed Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon made governor over the land.

footnotes.content: Ishmael came as a guest, eating bread with Gedaliah—the language of trust and covenant. But his heart was already bent toward murder, his royal blood burning with resentment. How many times does the Lord warn us that the one who breaks bread with us may break faith tomorrow?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In that moment, Gedaliah—the appointed vessel of mercy, set up by the king of Babylon to lead—fell by his own guest's sword. How swiftly human plans crumble when pride and vengeance move the hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The slaughter was complete—Jews and Chaldeans alike. Ishmael had no longer any allegiance to his own people, only to his rage. Such is the end of those who let bitterness root itself in their heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The day after the murders, no one yet knew. Evil often works in darkness, and discovery comes slowly. There is a mercy even in our ignorance, though it does not hold back the judgment that will follow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These pilgrims came from the north—Shechem, Shiloh, Samaria—bearing their mourning and their worship offerings. Even in exile's shadow, believing hearts still turn toward Jerusalem's temple. Their devotion was genuine, though their timing was terrible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ishmael went out weeping, his tears a lie—a mask of sorrow to draw the faithful into his trap. Oh, how the evil one can wear our sorrows as costume, using our own need to sympathize against us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Once they came into the city, Ishmael struck. The pilgrims fell into the very pit that Asa had dug long ago. The old place became a new grave, and judgment seemed to swallow up innocence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten men cried out, promising their stores of grain and oil—and Ishmael, moved by the prospect of provision, paused. Even in such darkness, the Lord's hand was not entirely withdrawn; mercy found a corner, though narrow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That pit had been made by Asa for fear of Baasha centuries before—a stronghold built by one king's anxiety. Now it holds the bodies of Ishmael's cruelty. The Lord takes up the old stones and uses them to reveal sin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ishmael seized the remnant—women, children, the king's daughters—and fled toward Ammon. He carried captives as though he were a victor, but he was only a brigand, an orphan of justice fleeing from the Lord's sight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Johanan heard. News travels, though evil tries to hide. The captains stirred themselves to pursue, and in that moment, the Lord was calling His people back to their own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gibeon's great waters became the place of reckoning. By those same waters, Joshua once commanded the sun to stand still. Now justice gathers its strength there again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the captives saw Johanan and his captains, they were glad—their faces turned toward rescue. Even the prisoners knew the difference between a predator and a deliverer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people turned about and came back. How quickly the grip of evil loosens when hope appears! They left Ishmael behind and moved toward Johanan—toward home, toward life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ishmael escaped with eight men into Ammon's land—a fugitive now, carrying nothing but the blood on his hands. His rage had consumed his own destiny, and he was left with only flight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Johanan recovered the remnant—the people, the women, the children, the eunuchs. He gathered the pieces that Ishmael had tried to scatter, becoming an instrument of the Lord's faithfulness even in dark hours.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They camped at Geruth Chimham by Bethlehem—the city of the great King's birth, though they did not yet know it. Even their flight carried them near the place where redemption would one day flower.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They feared the Chaldeans because of what Ishmael had done—fear of man's judgment chasing them into the night. Readers today hear an echo in that flight: how often do our anxieties drive us away from the very help the Lord offers us?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
